To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the magnitude and direction of inbreeding depression depend on genetic variation within and between stands and on the life-stage considered.

1) genetic diversity of wild cherry trees is highly variable across sites; 2) biparental inbred offspring have lower survival and growth rates than outbred offspring in some populations; 3) genetic diversity of pollen donors and mates is positively correlated with offspring performance in some populations; and 4) genetic diversity in wild cherry populations should be maintained for sustainable management.

(1) the genetic diversity of adult trees was strongly correlated with seedling diversity in one of the three stands, (2) biparental incompatibility was observed in two of the three stands and (3) in one of the stands, the incompatibility rate was positively correlated with the genetic diversity of both parents.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of genetic diversity on the survival of offspring, the effects of mating on the genetic diversity of offspring populations and on the consequences of these processes on the management of wild cherry populations.
the effects of mating systems on the maintenance of genetic diversity in natural populations and the implications for the conservation of genetic resources.
the conservation and sustainable management of wild cherry genetic resources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic diversity of P. avium stands and populations is not homogeneous and that the magnitude of biparentral inbreeding is variable among populations.
genetic diversity is not a panacea for all problems, but that its loss is a serious problem.
biparental inbred offspring have lower survival and growth in P. avum, and that the effects of biparental mating are more pronounced in stands with higher genetic diversity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic diversity in wild cherry is not as high as expected and the effects of genetic diversity on the offspring performance are variable across stands.
biparental incompatibility system in P. aviam may cause a strong inbreeding depression that can be alleviated by increasing the pollen donor diversity.

the genetic diversity of a stand is an important factor influencing the magnitude of inbreeding depression, which in turn affects the genetic composition and diversity of the next generation, and thus has consequences on the genetic diversity of the stand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biparental inbred depression is a major factor affecting the genetic diversity of P. avium populations.
the effects of mating systems on the genetic diversity and the consequences for offspring performance are not universal across populations, and should be tested at local scale.
the magnitude of inbreeding depression is not constant and depends on the genetic diversity of the stand.
